nameStory: This sleek blackbird is named after Thomas Mayo Brewer, a 19th-century ornithologist from Boston who studied New England birds. Brewer was a passionate egg collector and bird enthusiast who helped document many North American species, earning this western blackbird as his feathered namesake.
description: Brewer's Blackbird is a medium-sized songbird about the size of a robin, with males sporting glossy black feathers that shimmer with blue and green highlights in sunlight. Females are brownish-gray with darker wings and tail. These western birds are extremely rare visitors to New England, making any sighting a special treat for local birdwatchers.

idTips.label: Male's iridescent plumage
idTips.description: Males appear jet black from a distance, but up close their feathers gleam with rainbow-like blues and greens, especially on the head and neck, creating an oil-slick shimmer in good light

idTips.label: Bright yellow eyes
idTips.description: Both males and females have striking pale yellow eyes that stand out like tiny headlights against their dark plumage, quite different from the dark eyes of most other blackbirds

idTips.label: Straight, pointed bill
idTips.description: The bill is thinner and more needle-like than a grackle's, perfect for picking insects from grass and gleaning seeds from the ground

idTips.label: Square-ended tail
idTips.description: The tail appears fairly short and straight-edged when spread, lacking the long, wedge shape of grackles or the rounded tip of Red-winged Blackbirds

idTips.label: Ground-walking behavior
idTips.description: They walk confidently across open ground with a steady gait, rather than hopping like many songbirds, often in small flocks that move together like a coordinated search party

habitat: In their rare New England appearances, Brewer's Blackbirds typically show up in open areas like farm fields, large parking lots, or grassy areas near airports. They prefer short-grass habitats where they can easily walk and forage, often associating with other blackbird species in mixed flocks.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare vagrants might appear during migration, usually mixed in with flocks of other blackbirds returning north. Look for the distinctive yellow eyes among the crowd.
seasonality.summer: Breeding occurs far to the west, so summer sightings in New England would be exceptional strays. Any summer blackbird with yellow eyes deserves immediate documentation.
seasonality.fall: Fall migration offers the best chance for vagrant Brewer's Blackbirds in New England, when weather patterns occasionally push western birds eastward during their southward journey.
seasonality.winter: Very rarely, individuals might linger into early winter with mixed blackbird flocks, especially around agricultural areas with reliable food sources.

funFact: With only 2 recorded observations in all of New England, seeing a Brewer's Blackbird here is rarer than spotting many tropical vagrant birds – you'd have better odds of finding a wayward hummingbird from the western mountains!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with male Red-winged Blackbirds or Common Grackles, but the bright yellow eyes are the giveaway – Red-wings have dark eyes, and grackles have pale eyes but much longer, wedge-shaped tails and larger bills. Remember: 'Brewer's bright eyes' for the yellow peepers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being named after a New England ornithologist, Brewer's Blackbirds are quintessentially western birds that rarely venture east of the Great Plains. Any sighting in New England should be thoroughly documented and reported to birding authorities.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Rusty Blackbird, Brewer's males are more iridescent black (versus rusty-brown edges), and both species have yellow eyes, but Rusty Blackbirds are much more common in New England wetlands. Rusty Blackbirds also show more rusty-brown coloring in fall plumage, while Brewer's stay consistently dark.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rusty blackbirds can be distinguished from their close relative, Brewer's blackbird, by their preference for wet, forested habitats rather than open areas, and by their yellow eyes (Brewer's have dark eyes).
